newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian economy unaffected by campaign violence.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian economy unaffected by campaign violence.

text.p: Spiralling violence during the campaign for this week's Indonesian general elections has not affected the economy but it has raised problems which need to be addressed, economists said on Monday.
The four-week campaign culminated in rioting last Friday in the South Kalimantan town of Banjarmasin, where 142 people were killed in arson and street battles.
On the country's main Java island, clashes between rival political groups erupted frequently through the campaign, but there was little loss of life.

"For serious investors who know what they are doing -- I see no sign from what has been happening in the last few weeks to change their minds about the economy as it stands," said J.W. Taco Bottema, an economist with ESCAP, the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific.

"I see no reason to change the basic stand on the economy," he told Reuters. "In the short-term, we may have glitches and rampages and sometimes a riot, but there is no change in the medium-term picture."

Indonesia was calm on Monday mid-way through a five-day cooling off period before 125 million eligible voters go to the polls on Thursday. Analysts said the violence in Banjarmasin, on Borneo island, was an isolated outbreak and in the three days since there had been no reactions elsewhere. They also noted that most of those killed were people who were looting a shopping plaza and were trapped when it was set on fire.
The analysts said the most sensitive indicator of the country's economic health, the foreign exchange rate, was little affected by the violence.

"I think the impact on the market will not be significant because violence in the run-up to the election has been factored in," Pardi Kendy, treasury head of PT Bank Buana Indonesia, told Reuters on Sunday.
"Operators would be more scared if it (the Banjarmasin riot) had happened in Jakarta. We see the market here on Friday was relatively stable despite the widespread violence," he said.
On Monday, the rupiah firmed in slow trade to 2,440/41 against the dollar at 0925 GMT against a 2,440/42 opening.
Jakarta's Composite Index was up 4.673 points, or 0.71 percent, at 663.195.
Despite the confidence that the economy was on a sound footing, the analysts said the violence had raised some disturbing problems, mostly linked to long-term stability.
"The election violence highlights the need to deal with the sources of the violence," said Donald Hanna, an economist with Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong.
"Part of it is the question of perception as opposed to objective reality. On an objective basis people are better off, but objectivity is only part of the problem. Perceptions are another big part."

The reference was to a generally agreed belief that the violence during the campaign was an urban phenomenon driven by those who have been left behind by the rapid growth during President Suharto's three decades in power.
Analysts have said violence flared during the campaign because it was the one opportunity the country's rigid political system afforded for dissent.
"You have a political system that needs to adapt to the economic success of the past 30 years," Hanna added.

As well, analysts said, something had to be done to address foreign concerns about who would succeed Suharto, who is now 75, although in good health. "For the economy, the continuation of political stability is very important," said Aftab Raza, a senior Jakarta-based economist with the World Bank.
"The economy is still robust but there are some red signals...there is the question of succession."
